Expectation1: Meet sales targets set by management
Situation1: On the final day of the quarter, the team must hit the cumulative target to avoid penalties and secure bonuses.
Expectation2: Challenge unfair systems and influence policy change
Situation2: They raise concerns about a policy that seems to disadvantage certain youth, seniors, or refugee applicants.
Story: The phone in my hand felt heavier than usual as I dialed the next number on my list. As a telemarketer, today was the final push—management’s emails had been relentless, reminding us that missing the quarterly target meant no bonuses and possible penalties. My team was counting on me to close just a few more sales. But as I read the script, my other role tugged at me: the advocate who had spent months challenging the very policy I was now selling. I knew this policy’s fine print made it harder for young people and seniors to qualify, and I’d already raised concerns in meetings, arguing it was unfair and needed reform. Yet here I was, expected to convince someone—maybe a struggling student or a new immigrant—that this was their best option. My manager’s voice echoed in my mind, urging me to focus on the numbers, while my conscience whispered that I was betraying those I’d promised to help. My finger hovered over the call button, my heart pounding as I wrestled with the impossible choice between my job and my principles.
